summary: Defines Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC), a protocol for sending files reliably from one sender to a very large number of receivers at once, such as over multicast or broadcast. It combines layered coding transport, congestion control and forward error correction building blocks. It is a proposed standard that replaced RFC 3450.

plainLanguage.summary: ALC is a way to send one file to a very large audience over IP multicast. The file is chopped up and encoded so that lost pieces can be worked out from the pieces that arrive. Receivers never complain and never ask for anything: they simply collect until they have enough to rebuild the file.

questions: how to deliver files to many receivers with multicast
how does alc deliver files over multicast
what is the alc source packet indicator
subtitle: Reliable file delivery to a huge audience over multicast, with no feedback from receivers at all.

tldr.problem: Sending a file to millions of receivers over multicast is easy to start and hard to finish, because some packets will always be lost and asking for them back does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: ALC cuts the file into encoding symbols with an error-correcting code and sends them on several channels at different rates. A receiver just collects enough symbols to rebuild the file, and its own speed is set by which channels it stays joined to.
tldr.outcome: Every receiver gets the whole object at whatever speed its own path allows, and no receiver ever sends a message back to the sender. The document replaced RFC 3450 in 2010.

today: RFC 5775 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 3450 in 2010, moving the parts that belong to LCT in general into RFC 5651 and adding the Source Packet Indicator bit and the EXT_FTI header extension, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What ALC Is For
sections.content:
ALC is a massively scalable reliable content delivery protocol, designed to use IP multicast as its network service. Massive scalability here means that the number of concurrent receivers for an object may be in the millions, the aggregate size of the objects in a session ranges from hundreds of kilobytes to hundreds of gigabytes, each receiver can start receiving an object at any time, the reception rate of each receiver is the maximum fair bandwidth available between it and the sender, and all of this works from a single sender.

Because ALC is focused on reliable content delivery, the goal is to deliver objects as quickly as possible to each receiver while remaining friendly to competing traffic. The congestion control used with ALC should therefore make use of the available bandwidth while backing off aggressively when there is competition.

The protocol has four properties that make this work. To each receiver it appears as if there were a dedicated session from the sender to that receiver, with the reception rate adjusting to the congestion on that path. To the sender, there is no difference in load or outgoing rate whether one receiver or a million are joined, regardless of when they join and leave. No feedback packets are required from receivers to senders. And almost all the packets that pass through a bottleneck link are used by downstream receivers, sharing the link fairly with competing flows in proportion to their utility.

ALC is a protocol instantiation in the sense of RFC 3048, and it is deliberately minimal: it leaves out any application-specific feature that could limit its scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of ALC is scale. The sender does the same amount of work whether ten people are watching or ten million, and nobody watching ever sends anything back.

sections.title: The Three Building Blocks
sections.content:
ALC combines three building blocks. The LCT building block, RFC 5651, provides in-band session management. A multiple rate congestion control building block that complies with RFC 2357 provides congestion control without feedback: receivers adjust their reception rates individually by joining and leaving the channels of the session. The FEC building block, RFC 5052, provides reliability: the sender generates encoding symbols from the object and sends them, and receivers simply wait until they have received enough packets to reconstruct the object. There is no request for retransmission of individual packets, and the packets and their transmission rate are independent of the number of receivers and of what each receiver has experienced.

The definition of a session is the same as for LCT: multiple channels originating at a single sender, used for some period to carry packets for one or more objects. Congestion control is applied over the aggregate of the packets sent to all the channels of a session. A session is restricted to a single sender, but the same objects can also arrive from other senders in other sessions.

This document describes version 1 of ALC, which must use version 1 of LCT. ALC is defined as the payload of UDP over IP multicast, and it supports both IPv4 and IPv6 with no dependency on the IP version.
sections.plainLanguage: ALC is three standard pieces working together: one to label the packets, one to keep the speed fair, and one to encode the file so that losses can be repaired from the data that does arrive.

sections.title: The ALC Packet Format
sections.content:
An ALC packet is an IP packet, either IPv4 or IPv6, whose UDP header is followed by the LCT header, then the FEC Payload ID, then the packet payload, which holds the encoding symbols generated from the object. The Congestion Control Information field of the LCT header carries the information required by the multiple rate congestion control building block in use, and the FEC Payload ID identifies the encoding symbols in the payload so that the receiver knows how they were generated from the object.

The version number field of the LCT header must be interpreted as the ALC version number, and this version of ALC implicitly uses version 1 of the LCT building block. If more than one object is carried in the session, the Transmission Object Identifier in the LCT header must be used to say which object the symbols came from.

In some special cases a sender may produce packets with no payload at all, for example to signal the end of a session or to convey congestion control information. Such packets contain neither the FEC Payload ID nor any payload, and receivers detect their absence from the datagram length carried by the outer headers. For ALC the length of the Transport Session Identifier field is required to be non-zero, which means the sender must not set both the LCT flags S and H to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is a UDP datagram with three extra parts: the LCT header, an identifier for the coded piece inside, and the coded piece itself.

sections.title: Identifying the Session, the Object and the Kind of Packet
sections.content:
A Transport Session Identifier must be associated with each session and carried in the LCT header of every ALC packet. It is scoped by the sender's IP address, and the pair of sender address and TSI must identify the session uniquely. A Transmission Object Identifier must be used when more than one object is carried in a session, and it must be unique within the session, though not across sessions; if only one object is carried, the TOI may be omitted.

The LCT header also has a two-bit Protocol-Specific Indication field, in bits 6 and 7 of the first word. ALC uses bit X as the Source Packet Indicator and leaves bit Y reserved. The Source Packet Indicator is used with systematic FEC schemes that define a different FEC Payload ID format for packets holding only source data than for packets holding repair data: the indicator must be set to 1 when the source-data format is in use and to zero when the repair format is in use. For schemes with a single format, the sender must set it to zero and the receiver must ignore it. Two formats let the receiver carry only the FEC information that matters when decoding, and receivers that do not decode can ignore it.

ALC also defines a new LCT header extension, EXT_FTI, with extension type 64, whose content carries the encoded FEC Object Transmission Information for the object the packet belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet names the session it belongs to, and names the file if the session carries more than one. One spare bit in the header says whether the packet holds original data or repair data.

sections.title: The Session Description
sections.content:
Before a receiver can join an ALC session it needs a session description containing the multiple rate congestion control building block to be used, the sender's IP address, the number of channels in the session, the address and port number for each channel, the Transport Session ID to be used, an indication of whether the session carries packets for more than one object, the format of any header extensions to be used, and enough information to determine the packet authentication scheme if one is used.

The description may also carry the mapping between combinations of settings and Codepoint values, the data rate of each channel, the length of the packet payload, and information about each object, such as its Object Transmission Information and when it will be available.

The Codepoint field in the LCT header can carry some of the changing information inside a session. The session description then holds the mapping between Codepoint values and the settings they mean, so that, for example, a different FEC encoding algorithm for each object, or a different authentication scheme for each packet, can be signalled in band. How the session description is delivered is outside the scope of the document: it could be SDP, XML metadata, HTTP headers, a session announcement protocol, a web page, or email.
sections.plainLanguage: Before joining, a receiver is told the basics: which server, which channels, which congestion control scheme, and which file is which. The document does not say how that information is delivered.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
A sender should make the session description and the FEC Object Transmission Information available, and within a session it transmits a sequence of packets to the channels of the session at the rates the congestion control building block dictates. It must use the same TSI for all packets in the session, and when more than one object is delivered each object must have a unique TOI with the corresponding TOI used for all its packets. The FEC Payload ID must correspond to the encoding symbols in the payload.

On receipt, a receiver works through five steps in order. It parses the packet header and verifies that it is valid, discarding the packet if it is not. It verifies that the sender's IP address together with the TSI matches one of the pairs received in a session description to which the receiver is currently joined, and silently discards the packet if there is no match. It processes the CCI field in accordance with the congestion control building block. If more than one object is carried in the session, it verifies that the TOI is valid and discards the packet if it is not. And it processes the rest of the packet, using the FEC Payload ID and the encoding symbols in the payload to reconstruct the object.

Packet authentication is recommended. If it is used, the receiver should check the authenticity of a packet immediately, before the congestion control step, and silently discard the packet if the check fails.
sections.plainLanguage: Every arriving packet goes through the same checks: is the header sensible, is it from a session I joined, is the object one I want, and is it authentic. Only then does the receiver use the data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations that apply to the LCT, FEC and congestion control building blocks also apply to ALC. ALC is especially vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks in which forged packets are sent to the session, preventing or corrupting the reconstruction of the object, and it is particularly affected because many receivers may receive the same forged packet. The document recommends protection at both the application level and the packet level.

At the application level, an integrity check on the whole reconstructed object is recommended, ideally a digital signature the receiver can verify. If even one forged packet is used in the reconstruction, the object will usually be wrong, the check will fail, and the object should be discarded, so the acceptance of a single forged packet can still be an effective denial of service. The application-level check at least prevents the accidental use of a wrongly reconstructed object.

At the packet level, packet-level authentication is recommended, because corrupt or forged packets can then be discarded one by one and the authenticated ones used to rebuild the object, so the effect of an attack is proportional to the number of forged packets rather than to the size of the object. Packet-level authentication also protects the congestion control against forged packets carrying wrong congestion control information. Schemes such as TESLA cannot check a packet immediately, and in that case the receiver should check as soon as possible and discard the packet if it fails; if many packets fail, the receiver should delay its congestion control step until after the check. Reverse Path Forwarding checks should be enabled in the routers and switches along the path to limit the injection of forged packets.

The document also describes a baseline secure mode based on IPsec: transport mode, with the Encapsulating Security Payload protocol, data origination authentication enabled, confidentiality recommended, keys placed in advance, replay protection enabled, and automated key management recommended so that a rekey happens before the sequence space expires.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged packet can spoil the whole file for everyone who receives it, so the document asks for two checks: one on the finished file, and one on each packet as it arrives.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3450
sections.content:
The document lists the changes from the experimental RFC 3450. Material that applies to LCT in general, rather than to ALC alone, was moved into LCT, and material duplicated in LCT was removed. The references were updated to the new versions of the LCT and FEC building blocks, and the document was aligned with the changes in the new FEC building block. Normative and informative references were split.

The first bit of the Protocol-Specific Indication in the LCT header was defined as the Source Packet Indicator, used when an FEC scheme defines two FEC Payload ID formats so that packets holding only source symbols can be processed by receivers that do not support FEC decoding. The EXT_FTI LCT header extension was defined and registered with IANA. The intellectual property section was replaced with a standard statement.
sections.plainLanguage: The 2010 version moves the general parts of the protocol into the shared LCT document, fixes the references to the newer building blocks, and adds the one spare bit that says whether a packet holds original or repair data.

items.title: Looks like a dedicated session
items.text: Each receiver sees its own path to the sender, and its reception rate follows the congestion on that path.

items.title: No cost per receiver
items.text: To the sender, one receiver or a million make no difference to the load or the outgoing rate.

items.title: No feedback packets
items.text: Receivers never send anything back to the sender.

items.title: Fair sharing
items.text: Almost every packet through a bottleneck link is used by a downstream receiver, and the link is shared with competing flows in proportion to their use.

layers.label: LCT header
layers.detail: Session identifier, object identifier and congestion control information

layers.label: FEC Payload ID
layers.detail: Identifies the encoding symbols in the payload

layers.label: Encoding symbols
layers.detail: The coded form of the object

viz.caption: WHAT A RECEIVER DOES WITH EACH PACKET

items.title: 1. Parse the header
items.text: Check that the header is valid, and discard the packet if it is not.

items.title: 2. Check the session
items.text: The sender address and TSI must match a session the receiver has joined, or the packet is silently discarded.

items.title: 3. Run congestion control
items.text: Act on the CCI field as the congestion control scheme requires.

items.title: 4. Check the object
items.text: If the session carries several objects, the TOI must be valid, or the packet is discarded.

items.title: 5. Reconstruct
items.text: Use the FEC Payload ID and the encoding symbols in the payload to rebuild the object.

viz.caption: WHAT THE SESSION DESCRIPTION MUST SAY

items.title: Congestion control scheme
items.text: Which multiple rate congestion control building block the session uses.

items.title: Sender address
items.text: The IP address of the sender.

items.title: Number of channels
items.text: How many channels the session has.

items.title: Channel addresses and ports
items.text: The address and port number used for each channel.

items.title: Transport Session ID
items.text: The TSI to be used for the session.

items.title: One object or several
items.text: Whether the session carries packets for more than one object.

items.title: Header extension format
items.text: The format of the header extensions, if any are used.

items.title: Authentication scheme
items.text: Enough information to determine the packet authentication scheme, if one is used.
